On 11 December 1993 they were handed over to plain-clothed gendarmes from Diyarbakır. Mr Şahin had to pay for the air fares to Diyarbakır of himself, his wife and these officials. On arrival, the couple were detained at the provincial gendarmerie command. Mr Şahin alleged that he was tortured over 14 days, being given a quarter of a loaf of bread (about 200 g.) to eat a day. He did not see his wife during this time, nor was he informed of her fate. Prior to being brought to court, he was interrogated in the middle of the night and, after threats of rape had been made against his wife, he was made to scribble blindfolded on certain papers. He did not know their contents.

arguments.claim: The applicants alleged that their detention was unlawful and that they were tortured and ill-treated while in detention.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants, who are all Turkish lawyers, alleged that in November and December 1993 they were taken into detention by law enforcement officers on the pretext of involvement in criminal activities, but in reality because they had represented clients before the State Security Court and been involved in human rights work. They all claimed that their detention was unlawful (Article 5 of the Convention). Some of the applicants - Tahir Elçi, Şinasi Tur, Sabahattin Acar, Niyazi Çem, Mehmet Selim Kurbanoğlu, Meral Daniş Beştaş, Mesut Beştaş, Vedat Erten, and Hüsniye Ölmez - also claimed that they were tortured and otherwise ill-treated whilst in detention (Article 3).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found violations of Articles 3 and 5 concerning torture, ill-treatment, and unlawful detention.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the applicants were detained following incriminating statements by a PKK confessor and that they were treated in accordance with the law without ill-treatment.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the applicants were detained following incriminating statements by a PKK confessor and that they were treated in accordance with the law without ill-treatment.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicants' allegations credible and rejected the Government's claims of lawful detention and acceptable treatment.

arguments.claim: The applicants claimed that searches and seizures at the time of their arrests violated their rights under Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants Tahir Elçi, Şinasi Tur, Sabahattin Acar, Niyazi Çem and Mehmet Selim Kurbanoğlu made further complaints concerning the searches and seizures which took place at the time of the arrests (Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found violations of Article 8 and considered the complaints about seizures under Protocol 1 Article 1.

arguments.claim: The applicants alleged hindrance of their rights to make complaints to the Convention organs, engaging Article 34 (formerly Article 25).

anchor.surface_text: A further aspect of the case related to an alleged hindrance of the rights of Tahir Elçi, İmam Şahin, Arzu Şahin, Sabahattin Acar and Baki Demırhan to make complaints to the Convention organs (formerly Article 25 of the Convention, now Article 34).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no violation of Article 34 regarding hindrance of complaint rights.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the applicants' detention and treatment complied with the law and that no ill-treatment occurred.

anchor.surface_text: At no point were the applicants ill-treated. They were dealt with in accordance with the law and their conditions of detention were acceptable.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found credible evidence of torture and ill-treatment, rejecting the Government's claims.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court partly accepted that evidence obtained under duress should not be admissible but reserved some issues.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court emphasized the State's positive obligations to investigate and prevent torture and ill-treatment.

holdings.text: The Court rejects the Government's preliminary objection based on non-exhaustion of domestic remedies and holds that the applicants exhausted domestic remedies before lodging their applications.

anchor.surface_text: Preliminary objection rejected (exhaustion of domestic remedies)

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the applicants had exhausted domestic remedies before lodging their applications, rejecting the Government's preliminary objection.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention concerning the torture and ill-treatment of the applicants while in detention.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found credible evidence and accepted the applicants' allegations of torture and ill-treatment, rejecting the Government's claims of lawful treatment.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been a violation of Article 5 of the Convention regarding the lawfulness of the applicants' detention.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the detention was not lawful and did not comply with the requirements of Article 5, considering the lack of safeguards and disproportionality.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention and considers the complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning searches and seizures at the time of the applicants' arrests.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the searches and seizures violated the applicants' rights under Article 8 and considered the related property rights claims under Protocol 1 Article 1.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been no violation of Article 34 of the Convention (formerly Article 25) concerning the applicants' rights to make complaints to the Convention organs.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found no evidence that the applicants' rights to make complaints to the Convention organs were hindered, rejecting the claim of violation.

holdings.text: The Court partly accepts that statements and evidence obtained from the applicants under duress or torture are inadmissible in proceedings before the State Security Court, reserving some issues for further examination.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court partly accepted the applicants' argument that evidence obtained under duress should not be admissible, but reserved some issues for further consideration.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the respondent State failed to comply with its positive obligations under Article 3 to investigate and prevent ill-treatment of the applicants.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court emphasized the State's positive obligations under Article 3 and found that the State failed to effectively investigate and prevent the ill-treatment.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the margin of appreciation afforded to the State in matters of national security and detention was exceeded in this case, resulting in violations of the Convention.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the State exceeded its margin of appreciation by detaining and ill-treating the applicants without adequate safeguards.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the detention and restrictions on the applicants' rights were not necessary in a democratic society and were disproportionate, thus violating the Convention.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court applied proportionality and necessity tests and found that the detention and restrictions were not justified in a democratic society.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the proceedings before the State Security Court were criminal in nature according to the Engel criteria.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court applied the Engel criteria and determined that the proceedings before the State Security Court were criminal in nature.
